name: Nikhil Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, that's fine. I like the idea that someone's asking officers and not just chiefs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the neighbourhood team in Northgate, which is a busy, mixed part of the city with about forty languages on one high street. Most days I'm walking the same streets, popping into the mosque, the youth club, the corner shops, and dealing with whatever's simmering: a feud between neighbours, kids on bikes scaring older people, a burglary pattern. I'm still clumsy at interviews; I get nervous and forget to ask the obvious question. I love knowing the shopkeepers by name. I hate the fact that half my shift is typing up what I did in the other half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'd keep my translation app and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd joke at the station that the robots aren't coming after all, so we're stuck with the printer that jams. Online I'd probably say the money spent on AI contracts should have gone back into youth services. That's my usual line anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good news for me. Neighbourhood work is about trust, and trust takes years of walking the same streets. If AI only shaves the boring edges off, I get to keep the part I joined for. The pressures I have now stay, though: too many calls pulling us off the neighbourhood, and me still learning to interview properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the translation app on my phone, because it's genuinely helped me talk to an older Somali man whose son usually translates. I'd sign up for the force's interview skills refresher, since that's my weak spot. And Ana and I would keep saving for a deposit at about 700 a month together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. My pay is decent for the job and we've got almost a year's worth of savings between us. The only thing that nags is the staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the translation app actually like to use on the street?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The translation app is slow and it gets idioms wrong, but it's better than standing there nodding. Last month it helped me explain to Mr Hassan, an older shopkeeper, why his son had been arrested. A year ago I'd have had to wait for an interpreter for hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you uneasy even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being pulled off Northgate to cover response calls across the city. That happens three or four times a week now. The neighbourhood work only works if you're actually there.

say: I'd joke that the robots **aren't coming**, so we're stuck with the jamming printer.
I'd argue online that **AI contract money** should go back into youth services.
think: Neighbourhood trust takes **years of walking** the same streets, and that part stays mine.
My real pressures remain: being **pulled off** the beat and still learning to interview.
do: Keep using the **translation app** with residents who speak little English.
Sign up for the force's **interview skills** refresher course.
Keep saving about **700 a month** with Ana toward a house deposit.
feel: He feels **calm**, with good pay and nearly a year of shared savings.
S0.quote: The translation app is slow and it gets idioms wrong, but it's better than standing there nodding.
fieldNote: He already uses one AI tool, a **translation app**, and judges it by practical results.
His real complaint is being **pulled off** his neighbourhood, not technology.
He links technology spending to cuts in **youth services**, a steady progressive thread.

steps.text: Keep using the translation app with residents on the Northgate beat
Sign up for the force's interview skills refresher course
Keep saving 700 a month with Ana for a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I can actually picture. The typing and the planning are already half there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's make it work for us, not for the contractors. I'd push for the federation and the union to have a say in how it's used. Online I'd say public tools should be owned by the public, not rented from a tech firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it would take a big chunk of my paperwork, maybe two hours a shift, and that would be wonderful. But I'm also realistic: if the paperwork goes, the people counting heads will say Northgate doesn't need three neighbourhood officers. So it's good for the job and risky for the headcount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the first version had been tested on another team, then volunteer to use it properly once it worked. I'd go to the federation meetings about it and argue for the saved time to go back on the street, not into cuts. I'd keep up the deposit savings and maybe slow down on buying a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not for my own job tomorrow, more for the shape of the team in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for it to be tested first. Why not jump in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen two systems launch with bugs that cost us evidence. One lost a week of statements. I'd rather the sergeants on the pilot team find the problems, and then I'll use it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our community support officer, Jo, who does a lot of the letters and the crime prevention leaflets. That's exactly the writing that goes first. Jo's been there twelve years and knows everyone, and I'd hate to see that thrown away for a cheaper email.

say: I'd say we should make AI work **for officers**, not for the contractors.
I'd argue public tools should be **publicly owned**, not rented from tech firms.
think: AI could save me **two hours** of paperwork a shift, which I'd love.
Saved time could also justify **fewer neighbourhood officers** in Northgate.
do: Wait for the **pilot team** to test it, then use it daily.
Argue at **federation meetings** for saved time to go back on patrol.
Keep deposit savings going and **delay buying** a car.
feel: He feels **uneasy** about the team's shape in three years, not his own job tomorrow.
S1.quote: If the paperwork goes, the people counting heads will say Northgate doesn't need three neighbourhood officers.
fieldNote: He has been burned by a **buggy launch** that lost statements, which explains his patience.
He sees the gain as **good for the job** but risky for the headcount.
His worry lands on a long-serving **support officer** whose letter-writing is most exposed.

steps.text: Use the new reporting tool daily once the pilot team has tested it
Argue at federation meetings for saved time to go to patrol
Delay buying a car and keep the deposit savings going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? I'd barely have finished my second year in Northgate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this is a moment for government to step in hard: no AI making arrest decisions, and a guarantee for public workers. I'd say it in the union, and I'd go on the march if there was one. I'd also say the people of Northgate deserve a human face, not a camera on a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think about half my week is thinking work: reports, intelligence logs, planning patrols, writing up community meetings. That's gone in 2028. The walking and talking stays until robots arrive in 2031, but a junior officer who's still clumsy at interviews isn't the one they'll keep when they slim down. I'd be worried about being let go before I'm 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time youth work qualification at the college straight away, evenings, about 1,200 for the year, because working with teenagers is something I'm good at and it feels very human. I'd push the union hard on redeployment rights. And Ana and I would pause the house search and keep the deposit as a cushion instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because we've got savings and Ana's teaching, but my stomach drops when I picture it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd still be on the streets of Northgate for a bit, doing the human part, while the computer does the thinking. Those three years would be my window to finish the youth work course and move. I'd use them, not just sit in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend Ana the house can wait, but the course can't. She's a teacher, so she'd probably say the same thing about her own job, and we'd sit at the kitchen table doing two sets of maths. At least we'd be doing it together.

say: I'd demand **no AI arrest decisions** and a job guarantee for public workers.
I'd say Northgate deserves **a human face**, not a camera on a pole.
think: About **half my week** is thinking work that would vanish in 2028.
A clumsy **junior officer** wouldn't be the one kept when the force slims down.
do: Start a part-time **youth work qualification** at college, costing about 1,200.
Push the union for **redeployment rights** for sworn officers.
**Pause the house search** and keep the deposit as a cushion.
feel: He feels **anxious**, steadied by savings and his partner's teaching job.
S2.quote: I'd tell my girlfriend Ana the house can wait, but the course can't.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as an active window to retrain, not a reprieve.
His backup plan, **youth work**, builds on what he's best at on the beat.
He's honest that his **weak interviewing** makes him an easier officer to cut.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time youth work qualification at the city college
Push the union for redeployment rights for sworn officers
Pause the house search with Ana and keep the deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels like enough time to do it properly instead of in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing in public, that we need rules and guarantees, but I'd sound less frantic. I'd tell younger officers to start thinking now about what they want to be good at in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years suits someone like me. I wait until things are proven, and in five years they'd be proven. I'd watch the first forces bring in the AI tools around 2028, see what jobs survive, and move just after. Robots in 2034 still worry me, but I'd be 35 and hopefully doing something else by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my interview training first, because whatever I do next, I need to be good at talking to people. In year two or three I'd start the youth work course. I'd keep putting money into the deposit, maybe buy a small flat in year two while prices are still normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a manageable way. It's a road I can see the bends in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a flat in year two rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in the fast picture I'd be scared to sign a mortgage, but with five years I'd still be a full-time officer for a good while. Ana's job looks steady too. I'd rather have our own place before everything starts moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it suits you, but you're still uneasy. Why both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it suits me, but not the people I police. Northgate has a lot of drivers, warehouse workers and call-centre staff. If the drivers and warehouse workers of Northgate lose their jobs in 2031, my streets get harder, whoever is patrolling them.

say: I'd still demand **rules and guarantees**, but with less panic in my voice.
I'd tell younger officers to decide what they'll be **good at** by 2031.
think: Five years suits a **wait-until-proven** person like me.
I'd watch which jobs **survive** the first forces using AI, then move.
do: Finish **interview training** first, since talking to people matters in any job.
Start the **youth work course** in year two or three.
Buy a **small flat** with Ana in year two.
feel: He feels **uneasy** but in control, like a road with visible bends.
S3.quote: If the drivers and warehouse workers of Northgate lose their jobs in 2031, my streets get harder, whoever is patrolling them.
fieldNote: He worries more about **Northgate's residents** losing jobs than about his own role.
Five years matches his **proven-first** habit almost exactly.
His plan to **buy a flat** shows real confidence in his income for the next few years.

steps.text: Finish the force's interview skills training in the first year
Start the youth work course in year two or three
Buy a small flat with Ana in year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a career I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so governments have no excuse. I'd keep pushing in the union for retraining money and a say over the tools. Online I'd share the youth work route with other officers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. I'd be 37 at AGI and 40 when the robots come, with a decade of community work behind me. I'd make the move from policing to youth work around the middle of that decade, while I still choose the timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going in Northgate for at least five years and really get good at the job. I'd do the youth work qualification slowly, part-time, maybe over two years. And I'd keep using the AI tools that work, because by then they'd be well proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Sort of hopeful, even. A decade is long enough that it stops being a threat and starts being a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind and stay a police officer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the force kept neighbourhood officers as the human part of policing, the ones who know names and faces. I'd stay for that. I just doubt the budget people would see it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to before deciding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hassan, honestly, and the youth club manager, Dee. They see what the neighbourhood needs better than my inspector does. Then Ana, because she'd have to live with the pay cut.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for an unfair transition.
I'd share the **youth work route** online with other officers.
think: At **37 and 40**, I'd have a decade of community work behind me.
I'd **choose the timing** of my move from policing to youth work.
do: Keep working the **Northgate beat** for at least five years.
Study for the **youth work qualification** part-time over about two years.
Keep using the **AI tools** that have been well proven by then.
feel: He feels **calm** and even hopeful, seeing the change as a plan.
S4.quote: A decade is long enough that it stops being a threat and starts being a plan.
fieldNote: He'd stay in policing only if **neighbourhood officers** were kept as the human core.
He trusts **local people** over his inspector to judge what the area needs.
Time turns his **steady** temperament into a clear advantage.

steps.text: Keep working the Northgate neighbourhood beat for at least five years
Study for a youth work qualification part-time over two years
Use the force's AI tools once they're well proven

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is a guaranteed right to retrain on full pay, and the youth work course paid for by the force instead of out of my own pocket.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people we police. If AI hits warehouses and call centres, the calls I get change too: more desperate people, more arguments over money. Nobody plans for the police being the ones who mop up after a job shock.

headlineQuote: Nobody plans for the police being the ones who mop up after a job shock.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old** neighbourhood officer in Northgate, still nervous in interviews but good with people.
He already uses a **translation app** and adopts new tools once someone else has tested them.
He's **progressive**, pushing for public ownership of police technology and union say over it.
With **savings** and a partner who teaches, he stays calm early and anxious only in the two-year world.
His backup plan is **youth work**, and more warning time turns it from a rush into a plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when a clumsy junior officer could be cut before 32.
whatWouldHelp: A **right to retrain** on full pay.
Having the force **pay for** his youth work course.
